input:
It is well known that many decomposition reactions follow what is known as first-order kinetics, and the decomposition of the dye in the effluent that is considered here is a good example of this type of behaviour. In a first-order process, the rate at which the decomposition proceeds is directly proportional to the amount of the substance that is still present, which means that the decomposition is rapid at first and becomes progressively slower as time goes on. The rate constant $k$ for the dye has been found to be 0.098 per minute, and the question that we wish to answer is: what fraction of the dye will still remain after a period of 30 min has elapsed? The relationship between the fraction remaining and the time is given by the standard first-order decay law, in which $C$ represents the concentration at time $t$ and $C_0$ represents the initial concentration, and the law can be written in the following form:
$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$
If we now substitute the values that we have been given, namely $k$ = 0.098 per minute and a time of 30 min, into this equation, we obtain a value for the fraction remaining $C/C_0$ of 0.053. This means that, after 30 min, only a relatively small proportion of the original dye, corresponding to the fraction 0.053, will still be present in the effluent. It should, however, be pointed out that this result is based on the rate constant that was measured at one particular temperature, and since no activation energy is available, it is not possible to say how the result would change if the temperature were different.
target:
A dye in effluent decomposes by first-order kinetics. First-order kinetics means that the rate of decomposition at any moment is proportional to the concentration of dye still present: the more dye remains, the faster it decomposes, and the rate falls as the concentration falls. Determine the fraction of the dye remaining after 30 min. The rate constant $k$ for the decomposition is 0.098 per minute. The rate constant was measured at one temperature, and the value is used here at that temperature. The first-order decay law relates the fraction remaining to the rate constant and the time: where $C$ denotes the concentration at time $t$ and $C_0$ denotes the concentration at the start, the law is written
$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$
Substitution of $k$ = 0.098 per minute and a time of 30 min into the decay law gives the fraction remaining $C/C_0$ as 0.053. The calculation is a single substitution, because the law gives the fraction remaining directly once the rate constant and the time are fixed; no second relation and no iteration is needed. The result also fixes the shape of what follows: the decomposition continues at the same fractional rate; each further equal interval removes the same share of what is left, and the amount remaining is set by the accumulated time in the exponent rather than by the size of the residue at any one moment. The result can be checked against the limiting behaviour of the law: at the start the fraction remaining is the whole amount, and as time increases the fraction falls steadily towards zero without reaching it, so a small residue after half an hour is the behaviour the law leads one to expect. The fraction remaining, 0.053, is the share of the original dye still present at 30 min. The figure is valid at the temperature at which the rate constant was measured. No activation energy is available, so the rate constant cannot be corrected to another temperature, and the fraction at any other temperature is outside the reach of the stated data.
